title: TikTok as an Information Hodgepodge: Evaluation of the Quality and Reliability of Genitourinary Cancers Related Content
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of 61 genitourinary-cancer TikTok videos in which the authors (urologists) counted and typed 'obvious misinformation' in each video; 22/61 (36.07%) contained misinformation - a quantitative share of items judged inaccurate against clinical practice, with a stated denominator, i.e. a CONTENT prevalence estimate. The paper additionally reports quality-instrument shares (HONcode, DISCERN, Hexagonal Radar Schema) which are recorded as a QUALITY row per §3 and are not prevalence.

estimates.country: China (searches run on a phone set to Simplified Chinese; both International and Chinese/Douyin versions of TikTok; 57/61 sample videos in Mandarin Chinese, 4 in English)
estimates.measure_type: % of genitourinary-cancer TikTok videos containing obvious misinformation
estimates.value_raw: 22 posts (36.07%) were misinformative; Twenty-two videos (36.07%) had obvious misinformation (of 61 sample videos)
estimates.denominator: 61 TikTok videos on bladder, prostate and kidney cancer that met the inclusion criteria (of 167 retrieved on the first five pages of six keyword searches sorted most-watched first)
estimates.definition: Video recorded as containing at least one 'obvious misinformation' point by the two independent expert raters; types counted were quotation of outdated data/content (n=13, 21.31%), over-interpretation (n=5, 8.20%), implication of supernatural or heroic power such as self-healing (n=3, 4.92%), blurring the differences of numbers and proportions (n=3, 4.92%) and all-or-none thinking (n=1, 1.64%); some videos contained several errors
estimates.misinfo_def: "Numbers of obvious misinformation or ambiguous knowledge points on each video were recorded, and types of misinformation would be categorized." No formal definition of misinformation is given; the operational standard is contradiction of current clinical practice (e.g. "some videos would still recommend orchiectomy as a major method for endocrinotherapy ... which contradicts real-world practice")
estimates.source_quote: Twenty-two videos (36.07%) had obvious misinformation. Some contained several errors. The most common type was the quotation of outdated data and content (n = 13, 21.31%), followed by over-interpretation (n = 5, 8.20%), the implication of supernatural or heroic power such as the self-healing of the disease (n = 3, 4.92%), blurring the differences of numbers and proportions (n = 3, 4.92%), and all-or-none thinking (thinking in an extremism way, n = 1, 1.64%).
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Video Content and Information Quality', p. 4 (also Abstract and Discussion 'Major Findings')
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two authors (urologists at Peking Union Medical College Hospital) independently evaluated every video and a third author computed mean scores; misinformation points were counted and categorised against current clinical practice. No inter-rater reliability statistic, and no written rubric for what counts as 'obvious misinformation', is reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: A comprehensive search was conducted on TikTok (both International and Chinese versions) from 13th to 20th September 2021. Keywords were "bladder cancer", "prostate cancer", "kidney cancer", "hematuria", "elevated PSA", and "back pain". To simplify the sample collecting process, the results of each keyword we used would be sorted from the most-watched to the least. All relevant videos on the first five pages of the information flow will be downloaded. As a result, a total of 167 videos were retrieved.
estimates.notes: The denominator is the 61 INCLUDED videos, not the 167 retrieved: 106 were dropped before coding as commercial (43), irrelevant (27), pirated (12) or incomplete (9). This inflates the misinformation share relative to the retrieved set, and the authors note that 'some excluded commercial videos contained disinformation, such as exaggerating the efficacy of products and creating anxiety' - so the 36.07% excludes an unquantified amount of commercial disinformation. breadth coded 'misleading' (the broadest tier) because the numerator mixes outright factual error (outdated data) with over-interpretation and number/proportion confusion. Type shares were not split into separate rows: they are sub-categories of the pooled 36.07% and sum to 25 error instances across 22 videos.

estimates.country: China (searches run on a phone set to Simplified Chinese; both International and Chinese/Douyin versions of TikTok; 57/61 sample videos in Mandarin Chinese, 4 in English)
estimates.measure_type: % of genitourinary-cancer TikTok videos scoring no more than 5 points on the HONcode scale (poor to mediocre quality)
estimates.denominator: 61 TikTok videos on bladder, prostate and kidney cancer that met the inclusion criteria
estimates.definition: Video scored <=5 of 8 points on the Health on the Net (HONcode) code-of-conduct scale, which the authors read as 'somewhere between poor and mediocre' quality; the scale rates understandability, accessibility and credibility of health information, not truth or falsity
estimates.misinfo_def: n/a - quality instrument, not a veracity judgement
estimates.source_quote: Most videos (n = 59, 96.72%) scored no more than 5 points in the HONCode scale, meaning that the quality of most videos on TikTok was somewhere between poor and mediocre.
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Video Content and Information Quality', p. 4 (also Abstract)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two authors independently applied the HONcode (8 principles), the Hexagonal Radar Schema (6 dimensions, 0-2 points each) and the DISCERN instrument; a third author averaged the verdicts. No inter-rater reliability statistic reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: The HONCode is a code of conduct comprising eight procedural principles that aim to assist users in identifying the understandability, accessibility, and credibility of health information on a website (8, 9).
estimates.notes: QUALITY row per §3 (kept, excluded from prevalence). A wholly accurate video can score <=5 on the HONcode - the scale rewards transparency, sourcing and attribution rather than veracity - so this is not a misinformation share. Included because it is one of the paper's two headline results; the companion DISCERN result is a mean (2.41 of 5), not a share, and the Hexagonal Radar results are per-dimension completeness shares (symptoms 59.02%, examinations 54.10%, definition and outcomes tied at 21.31%), i.e. coverage, not veracity.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (1) DISCERN results - reported only as means (overall 2.41/5; by uploader type in Tables 2-4), so scale scores with no share, no row. (2) Hexagonal Radar Schema per-dimension shares ('more than half of the videos delivered moderate to high quality (> 1 point) content on the symptoms (n = 36, 59.02%) and examinations (n = 33, 54.10%)'; 'the diseases' basic definitions and outcomes were less discussed (n = 13, tied at 21.31%)') - these are content-COVERAGE shares on a completeness scale, not veracity, and a fully accurate video can score 0 on a dimension it simply does not mention; kept out to avoid double-counting the QUALITY row. (3) '53 videos (86.89%) had at least two unexplained medical terms' - readability, not veracity. (4) Uploader-type shares (healthcare practitioners n=29, 47.54%; media agencies n=19, 31.15%; hospitals n=8, 13.11%; patients n=3, 4.92%) are sample composition, not misinformation. (5) The 63.47% pre-coding exclusion rate (commercial 40.57%, irrelevant 25.47%, pirated 11.32%, incomplete 8.49%) - screening attrition, not a misinformation share, though it matters for interpreting the 36.07% (see the row's notes). (6) Third-party figures quoted in the Discussion - 'nearly one-third of them were misleading' (ref 15), '71.8% of patients would search health information online' and the 85.9%/14.1% split (ref 16), 'more than 40% of patients reported histories of quitting treatment based on advice from social media' (ref 17), 'approximately half of the videos on YouTube about prostate cancer contain undefined medical terms' - all cited from elsewhere, excluded by R8. Uncertainty flagged for the adjudicator: country coding. The phone was set to Simplified Chinese and 93.44% of the sample was Mandarin, so I coded China/single, but the search covered 'both International and Chinese versions' of the app and four videos were in English, so a Global/global coding is defensible.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis of TikTok (International and Chinese versions), 13-20 September 2021, from a wiped smartphone with location services on and activity tracking off, language Simplified Chinese; six keywords ('bladder cancer', 'prostate cancer', 'kidney cancer', 'hematuria', 'elevated PSA', 'back pain'), results sorted most-watched first, all relevant videos on the first five pages downloaded; 167 videos retrieved, 106 excluded (commercial 43, irrelevant 27, pirated 12, incomplete 9), 61 analysed; two authors independently rated every video (HONcode, Hexagonal Radar Schema, DISCERN) and counted/typed misinformation points, with a third author averaging verdicts; NO inter-rater reliability statistic and no misinformation rubric reported; univariate ANOVA with post-hoc LSD by uploader type; single-language, single-week snapshot; three uploader categories had n=1-3, and the two n=1 categories were dropped from some analyses.
rob.item6_quote: In this article, we defined every downloaded video as an independent. Numbers of obvious misinformation or ambiguous knowledge points on each video were recorded, and types of misinformation would be categorized.
rob.item10_quote: Amongst 61 sample videos, healthcare practitioners contributed the most content (n = 29, 47.54%). However, 22 posts (36.07%) were misinformative, and the most common type was using outdated data.
